                    ### Question
                    A 16-year-old male is brought to the clinic by his mother for the complaints of fever, nonproductive cough, fatigue, lack of appetite, and sore throat for the past 2 months.  Several other students at his high school have had similar symptoms. Physical exam shows a whitish membrane in his oropharynx, bilateral enlarged cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly.  Which of the following tests is most likely to diagnose his condition.?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Throat culture
opb. Chest X-ray
opc. Urine culture
opd. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
ope. Monospot test

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 16-year-old male, including fever, nonproductive cough, fatigue, lack of appetite, sore throat, whitish membrane in the oropharynx, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly, is highly suggestive of infectious mononucleosis, commonly caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The Monospot test is a rapid diagnostic tool that detects heterophile antibodies and is specifically used for diagnosing infectious mononucleosis, making it the most appropriate test in this scenario. Other options, such as throat culture and urine culture, are less relevant as they do not specifically diagnose mononucleosis. The presence of similar symptoms in other students supports the viral etiology, further aligning with the consensus that the Monospot test is the best diagnostic choice for this condition.
